# Theorem
Let $p$ be a prime. The set $\mathbb{Q}_p$ of $p$-adic numbers is uncountable.

## Setup and conventions
For $r\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ write $r=p^{k}\,a/b$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ not divisible by $p$; the $p$-adic norm is $|r|_p=p^{-k}$, and $|0|_p=0$. It is well defined, multiplicative, and satisfies the ultrametric inequality $|r+s|_p\le\max(|r|_p,|s|_p)$.

$\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the completion of $(\mathbb{Q},|\cdot|_p)$: its elements are equivalence classes of $|\cdot|_p$-Cauchy sequences of rationals, where $(u_N)\sim(v_N)$ iff $|u_N-v_N|_p\to 0$. (Equivalently, $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is a complete valued field containing $\mathbb{Q}$ densely with norm extending $|\cdot|_p$; the argument below adapts verbatim, see the Remark.)

A set $S$ is countable if there is an injection $S\to\mathbb{N}$.

## Step 1: $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is uncountable
Let $B=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of sequences $x=(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_n\in\{0,1\}$. Suppose $j:B\to\mathbb{N}$ were injective. Fix $e\in B$ and define $g:\mathbb{N}\to B$ by $g(k)=j^{-1}(k)$ if $k\in j(B)$ and $g(k)=e$ otherwise; $g$ is surjective. Define $z\in B$ by $z_n=1-g(n)_n$. For every $n$, $z_n\ne g(n)_n$, so $z\ne g(n)$. Hence $z\notin g(\mathbb{N})=B$, a contradiction. So $B$ is uncountable.

## Step 2: an injection $B\to\mathbb{Q}_p$
For $x\in B$ and $N\ge0$ put
$$s_N(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}x_np^n\in\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Q}.$$

**Cauchy.** For $M>N$, by the ultrametric inequality (applied inductively) and $|x_n|_p\le 1$,
$$|s_M(x)-s_N(x)|_p=\Big|\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}x_np^n\Big|_p\le\max_{N<n\le M}|x_n|_p\,p^{-n}\le p^{-(N+1)},$$
which tends to $0$ as $N\to\infty$. So $(s_N(x))_N$ is Cauchy, and we set $\varphi(x)=[(s_N(x))_N]\in\mathbb{Q}_p$.

**Injective.** Let $x\ne y$ in $B$ and let $m$ be the least index with $x_m\ne y_m$, so $x_m-y_m=\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. For $N\ge m$,
$$s_N(x)-s_N(y)=\sum_{n=m}^{N}(x_n-y_n)p^n=p^m\big(\varepsilon+p\,t_N\big),\qquad t_N=\sum_{n=m+1}^{N}(x_n-y_n)p^{\,n-m-1}\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
The integer $\varepsilon+p\,t_N$ is congruent to $\pm1$ modulo $p$, hence not divisible by $p$ (as $p\ge2$), and in particular nonzero. Therefore $|s_N(x)-s_N(y)|_p=p^{-m}$ for all $N\ge m$. This does not tend to $0$, so $(s_N(x))\not\sim(s_N(y))$, i.e. $\varphi(x)\ne\varphi(y)$.

## Step 3: conclusion
If $\mathbb{Q}_p$ were countable, with injection $\iota:\mathbb{Q}_p\to\mathbb{N}$, then $\iota\circ\varphi:B\to\mathbb{N}$ would be injective, contradicting Step 1. Hence $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$

**Remark (abstract completion).** If $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is taken as any complete field with absolute value $|\cdot|_p$ extending that of $\mathbb{Q}$, let $\varphi(x)=\lim_N s_N(x)$ (exists by completeness and the Cauchy estimate). By the reverse triangle inequality $\big||a|_p-|b|_p\big|\le|a-b|_p$ the norm is continuous, so $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|_p=\lim_N|s_N(x)-s_N(y)|_p=p^{-m}\neq0$, giving injectivity again.
